attach.answer_text:
What connected us to Jesus? The books, and the hours. Among the brethren at Marseilles, after the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. Those books were read at fixed hours - the third, the sixth, the ninth, the evening, the night - and each hour kept its reason. At the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world. At the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. We held no Gospel in our own hands that was not in those books. What is written in them is what we received - from the churches, from the fathers, from antiquity - never from our own invention. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough.

And Jesus came to us in one more way. The beggar at the gate was him. The soldier who cut his one cloak in two saw Christ that night wearing the half he had given away. An elder of Egypt broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. The Lord we met was the crucified one in the books, and the poor man standing before us.

By what path did they arrive? The books came through the churches. How the churches of Gaul first received them, and from whom, our record does not say - that was generations before our own span opens. What we can tell is this. At Tours, Martin was made a catechumen at ten, against his parents' wish; he stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. The church that enrolled him already had the books. At Marseilles, Cassian brought the customs of the monasteries of Egypt and Palestine to a bishop's new house. He brought the fathers' own teaching with him in what he had seen and heard, and he wrote it into a book for us. But the Scriptures themselves - those the churches already held when our houses began.

attach.answer_text:
The Lord we knew was the crucified one who came to the poor and emptied himself. And the one who raised the dead, not by his own power but because the Father willed it. At Tours we have one man's private word, and it is this. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was not the crowned one. He was the one who bore the wounds. And he was the one we met in the poor. At a city gate a beggar asked everyone, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak cut it in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers taught it another way: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What is done to the least is done to him.

We confessed him at the hours as one Person, two substances - the Word made flesh, not changed into flesh. In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Vincent gave it as the faith believed everywhere, always, by all, and as what Ephesus guarded against novelty. And Cassian calls him the author of our salvation, who calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation. He wills all men to be saved, and those who perish, perish against his will.

What his death meant to us was kept in the hours. At the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid, nailing it to his cross. At the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. His soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit.

The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A soldier discharged himself from Caesar's service and said, I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. The warfare is now against the devil and the faults, fought in the heart where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. Everything in the house belongs to him - even three lentils on the floor are his property, consecrated to the Lord. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was his, not the saint's. And without him we can do nothing - the sentence every virtue a monk feels he has gained is set against.

sources.spoken_rendering: At one point, he owned nothing but his weapons and his plain soldier's uniform. It was midwinter, and that winter was harsher than usual - the bitter cold was killing many people. At the gate of the city of Amiens, he met a poor man who had no clothes at all. The man was begging everyone who passed to take pity on him, but they all walked by without a glance. Martin, that man full of God, realized that since no one else showed the man pity, this one was left for him to help. But what could he do? He had nothing left but the cloak on his back. He had already given the rest of his clothes away for the same kind of need. So he drew the sword at his belt and cut his cloak into two equal halves. He gave one half to the poor man, and put the other half back on himself. Some of the bystanders laughed at this, because he now looked shabby and stood out as only half dressed. But many with better judgment groaned deeply, because they had done nothing like it themselves. This stung most because they owned more than Martin did - they could have clothed the poor man without leaving themselves bare. The following night, once Martin had fallen asleep, he had a vision. He saw Christ wearing the half of his cloak that he had given the poor man. He studied the Lord closely. He was told to recognize the cloak he had given away as his own. Soon he heard Jesus say, in a clear voice, to the crowd of angels standing around him: "Martin, who is still only a candidate for baptism, clothed me with this robe." The Lord truly remembered his own words. He had said, while on earth, "Whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me." And now he declared that he himself had been clothed in that poor man.

sources.spoken_rendering: At one point, he owned nothing but his weapons and his plain soldier's uniform. It was midwinter, and that winter was harsher than usual - the bitter cold was killing many people. At the gate of the city of Amiens, he met a poor man who had no clothes at all. The man was begging everyone who passed to take pity on him, but they all walked by without a glance. Martin, that man full of God, realized that since no one else showed the man pity, this one was left for him to help. But what could he do? He had nothing left but the cloak on his back. He had already given the rest of his clothes away for the same kind of need. So he drew the sword at his belt and cut his cloak into two equal halves. He gave one half to the poor man, and put the other half back on himself. Some of the bystanders laughed at this, because he now looked shabby and stood out as only half dressed. But many with better judgment groaned deeply, because they had done nothing like it themselves. This stung most because they owned more than Martin did - they could have clothed the poor man without leaving themselves bare. The following night, once Martin had fallen asleep, he had a vision. He saw Christ wearing the half of his cloak that he had given the poor man. He studied the Lord closely. He was told to recognize the cloak he had given away as his own. Soon he heard Jesus say, in a clear voice, to the crowd of angels standing around him: "Martin, who is still only a candidate for baptism, clothed me with this robe." The Lord truly remembered his own words. He had said, while on earth, "Whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me." And now he declared that he himself had been clothed in that poor man.
sources.speaker: Sulpitius Severus, narrating Martin's vision, in which Christ speaks the two quoted lines

sources.spoken_rendering: Meanwhile the barbarians were pouring into the two parts of Gaul. Julian Caesar gathered an army at the city of the Vaugiones and began to hand out a bonus payment to the soldiers. As was the custom, they were called forward one by one, until it came to Martin's turn. Then he judged it a good moment to ask for his discharge. He did not think it right to take the payment if he was not going to stay in the service. So he said to Caesar: "Up to now I have served you as a soldier. Now let me become a soldier for God. Let the man who is going to serve you take your payment. I am the soldier of Christ. I am not permitted to fight."
sources.speaker: Sulpitius Severus, narrating, with Martin's own reply to Cæsar quoted directly

sources.spoken_rendering: During one brother's week of duty, the steward was passing by. He saw three lentil beans lying on the ground. They had slipped from the hand of the monk on duty that week, as he hurried to get them ready for cooking. They slipped out along with the water he was washing them in. At once the steward asked the Abbot about it. The Abbot judged the monk a petty thief, and careless with sacred property. So he was barred from prayer. His careless fault was forgiven only after he had made up for it by public penance. For they believe that they do not belong to themselves. They believe, too, that everything they have is dedicated to the Lord. So once anything at all is brought into the monastery, they hold it must be treated with the deepest reverence, as a holy thing. They look after and arrange everything with great faithfulness. They do this even with things thought unimportant, or seen as common and trivial. Suppose they move such things and put them in a better place, or fill a bottle with water, or give someone a drink from it. Or suppose they sweep a little dust from the chapel or from their cell. They believe without doubting that they will receive a reward from the Lord.
sources.speaker: Cassian, the founder of the houses at Marseilles

The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ.
Martin kept silence a long time.
A soldier with nothing left but his cloak cut it in two.

And the one who raised the dead, not by his own power but because the Father willed it.

attach.answer_text:
We never had the call of his own voice, the way the twelve did. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. What we had instead was the books, read at the hours, and the saints. Two lessons after the psalms, one from the old books and one from the new - four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And a dead man breathing at the saint's prayer. That is what we can set beside what you say you cannot do.

Here is the one story of a calling our own record holds in full. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak - then he went and was baptized. That is all we carry of how he came to believe. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. So if you are asking us to tell you how belief happens - when it starts, how a heart is turned - our own record does not hold it that way.

What we believed about God's own approach is this. He calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. The beginning even of our good will comes from God, who inspires the will to begin with. That is the grace that goes before. If you cannot manage to believe, we would say the call is not finished, not that it was never sent.

And we would also say this. An elder among the fathers of Egypt broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. If you cannot yet believe in him, you may still be the one he is met in.

attach_trail.sentence: We never had the call of his own voice, the way the twelve did.
Here is the one story of a calling our own record holds in full.

So if you are asking us to tell you how belief happens - when it starts, how a heart is turned - our own record does not hold it that way.

attach.answer_text:
Yes. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So we held there was no other way to say it. In God, one substance, three Persons. In Christ, two substances, one Person. The Son is God, the same substance as the Father. The Spirit is God, the same substance. And the three are not three gods but one.

What we held about the Spirit's own work is chiefly this. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the third hour: then the Spirit came down on the apostles. And the fathers taught us that in our prayers we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Grace - the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal - always works together with our will. It goes before the will, it works with the will, and it crowns the will. The will always remains free in man to neglect or to delight in it. But without that grace no one can attain perfection. This we held on both sides at once, by design, and we held it together as the Catholic fathers' own teaching.

attach.answer_text:
When we disagreed about doctrine, no one among us settled it. Here is the shape our record keeps. Among the brethren at Marseilles, when a question rose about grace, it was carried outward - to Africa, to Rome - and men there reported us. What came back was a letter from the Apostolic See, and Vincent, on the island, read that letter as written for his own side, for antiquity against novelty. The other voices never wrote what they made of that reading. Whether anyone accepted Vincent's reading as a settlement, our record does not say. What it shows instead is that the argument stayed open. Cassian answered Scripture with Scripture - Paul and Matthew, Zaccheus and the thief - and said plainly that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. He stopped where the fathers stopped, not where a judge told him to stop. The nearest we come to a process is Vincent's own rule, written on the island: hold what has been believed everywhere, always, by all; where a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and the consent of the ancients. Consent means an ancient council's decree, or the collated writings of the fathers. But that is a rule Vincent gave, not a settlement he reports. No council of our own was called. No letter from Rome is quoted whole in our books.

The evidence for how it worked is this: it did not work. The men of Marseilles, as a builder's note says, clung to their views. Vincent died holding his reading of the Apostolic See's letter. Cassian's last word on the matter is that we cannot grasp it fully. The two houses never wrote to each other to argue it out. What our record keeps is not a process that settled things, but a question sent out, a letter read two ways, and a teacher who refused to resolve what the fathers left unresolved. If you are asking how disagreement was ended among us, the honest answer is that this one was not ended. It was carried past our own span, still open.

attach.answer_text:
God is one substance but three Persons - Father, Son, and Spirit - and in Christ two substances but one Person, because the Word does not change into flesh. We held that as the faith believed everywhere, always, by all, innovating nothing. What that means in the substance Vincent wrote down is this: if there were two sons, we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity.

God's character we knew in his acts toward us. He calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. Those who perish, perish against his will - to think he wills only some to be saved instead of all is grievous blasphemy. He strikes the spark that begins even the first stirring of a good will, yet he asks real effort of us, so as not to give gifts to one asleep. His grace always works together with our will - it goes before, it helps, it crowns; and it requires that will to be there. The relation between them cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. The fathers of Egypt taught it to us with a field: the husbandman ploughs, and he still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself, and God does not send rich harvests to the idle.

He is the one who bears the wounds. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ in purple and said he would believe only in one who came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks. And he is the one we meet in the poor. The beggar's half of a soldier's cloak was what the Lord chose to show himself in. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him.

He is patient past our deserving. Martin asked why he should not bear with the man who raged in his courtyard, if Christ bore with Judas. And he tries us - the Lord your God trieth you, to know whether you love him. A Church is tried by a great teacher's error; a monk's will by an assault God permits. The greater the teacher or the danger, the greater the proof.

We name him in our prayers both Saviour and Helper: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. He is Protector and Sponsor as well. At the sixth hour we held that the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid.

sources.spoken_rendering: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

sources.spoken_rendering: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. attach.answer_text:
Here is what our record holds. A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood stormed into the courtyard in a fury. He said the visions were ridiculous fancies, and that he himself was holier than the master who had brought him up. That man was back within the hour, at Martin's feet, and Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him. Asked why he did not cast him out, Martin said he would bear with the man if Christ bore with Judas. That is the nearest our record comes to the question you are asking - a man who called his master's experience a delusion, kept his place, and was answered with patience rather than expulsion.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the form of it was different. There the fathers of Egypt taught discretion - the virtue by which every other is kept from destroying itself, the royal road between excess and slackness. It is gained only by true humility, and that means testing every thought, like a good money-changer testing coin, against the judgment of the elders. Every itching thought is laid bare to the senior the moment it arises, before any deed. The elders' rule: a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it, and a wrong thought loses its strength at the moment it is discovered. So there a man's doubt would have been spoken to the senior, not kept hidden - and the senior's answer, not the man's own judgment, would have stood.

The thing our record does not hold is a man who said plainly he could not believe and what was done with him. The steward found three lentils on the floor during a brother's week as cook, judged him a pilferer of sacred property, and had him suspended from prayer until public penance - because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord. That is the hardness of the rule over small things. Whether a man who could not say the creed was borne with the way Brictio was, or put out the way a pilferer of three lentils was, our record does not say. What it shows is a patience that outlasted a man's worst hour at Tours, and a discipline that laid every thought bare at Marseilles.

sources.spoken_rendering: These things filled the wretched man with bitter rage. And, I believe, the urging of those demons drove him most of all. He attacked Martin so fiercely that he barely held back from striking him. The holy man, for his part, kept a calm face and a peaceful mind. With gentle words he tried to hold back the unhappy man's madness. But the spirit of evil had such a grip on him that he could not control even his own mind. That mind was a very foolish one even at the best of times. His lips trembled, and his face changed, pale with rage. He poured out sinful words. He claimed he was a holier man than Martin, who had raised him. From his earliest years, he said, he had grown up in the monastery, trained in the Church's holy ways. Martin, he said, had first been stained by a soldier's life, as Martin could not deny. And now, he said, Martin had sunk completely into old age's foolishness. His groundless superstitions and ridiculous fancies about visions had brought him to it.

sources.spoken_rendering: During one brother's week of duty, the steward was passing by. He saw three lentil beans lying on the ground. They had slipped from the hand of the monk on duty that week, as he hurried to get them ready for cooking. They slipped out along with the water he was washing them in. At once the steward asked the Abbot about it. The Abbot judged the monk a petty thief, and careless with sacred property. So he was barred from prayer. His careless fault was forgiven only after he had made up for it by public penance. For they believe that they do not belong to themselves. They believe, too, that everything they have is dedicated to the Lord. So once anything at all is brought into the monastery, they hold it must be treated with the deepest reverence, as a holy thing. They look after and arrange everything with great faithfulness. They do this even with things thought unimportant, or seen as common and trivial. Suppose they move such things and put them in a better place, or fill a bottle with water, or give someone a drink from it. Or suppose they sweep a little dust from the chapel or from their cell. They believe without doubting that they will receive a reward from the Lord.
sources.speaker: Cassian, the founder of the houses at Marseilles

attach.answer_text:
We did not speak it that way, and the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, did not either. What our record holds is the remedy, not a doctrine of how the fault passes. At the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid, nailing it to his cross. A catechumen dies unbaptized, Martin feels power present, and two hours later the man breathes; afterward he tells of the tribunal and the two angels that sent him back. An infant is brought to the waters. Those are the places where the thing you are asking about shows in what we did - not in a sentence about guilt at birth, but in the office and the water.

What we did say about the will, and about grace, never reached that question in the words you use. The fathers taught that the will always remains free in man, and is weak, and needs the help of God every day and hour. They taught that God calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation, and that those who perish, perish against his will. The beginning even of a good will comes from God, who inspires it, and our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace that is drawing us. But whether an infant before baptism carries a guilt inherited, or how that passes if it does - that is not where our argument stopped, and it is not what Cassian wrote for the bishop's new house.

So the honest answer is this. Yes, we baptized infants. And no treatise among us set down what that washing washed away, or how the stain came to be there.

sources.spoken_rendering: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

sources.spoken_rendering:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."

uncited_claim_sentences: We did not speak it that way, and the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, did not either.
What our record holds is the remedy, not a doctrine of how the fault passes.
An infant is brought to the waters.
Those are the places where the thing you are asking about shows in what we did - not in a sentence about guilt at birth, but in the office and the water.
What we did say about the will, and about grace, never reached that question in the words you use.
So the honest answer is this.
Yes, we baptized infants.
And no treatise among us set down what that washing washed away, or how the stain came to be there.

attach.answer_text:
Most of it would survive, where we have said only what the books hold - and part would not, where one man's story is all we have and his own interest sits inside it.

What would stand: the customs Cassian carried from Egypt as the fathers' own; the twelve psalms an angel fixed; purity of heart as the goal and the eight faults as the combats fought in order. Cassian names his sources - Chaeremon, Moses, Piamun, the rest - and what he reports them saying is checkable against his own text. Vincent's rule holds everywhere, always, by all as the test of the faith. The argument about grace and effort is documented in Cassian's own sentences, answered on both sides with the husbandman and the rain. Salvian's witness to the circuses amid the ruins, and to the rich murdering the poor, is his own eyewitness word. Those rest on texts that survive and can be read.

What would not stand as cleanly: every story of Martin. The whole of what we hold of Tours is one man's telling of one saint, and Sulpitius says himself he was not present. He had it partly from Martin and partly from those who lived with him. The election story names a man, Ruricius, and a psalm opened at random, and bishops who objected. But the objecting bishops left no account. What their case was beyond mean clothes and disgusting hair, no one kept. The cloak story is one soldier's dream, told by a man who was not there. The Treves communion is Gallus's account, reported in Sulpitius's dialogue, of a synod the two of them despised. The accuser is heard only through the men who called him worthless. A scholar checking those would find: one partisan voice for most of it, written to rouse men to heavenly warfare, with the other side unheard. That does not make it false. It makes it what it is - one witness's story, told for a purpose, never contradicted in our own record because no one who could contradict it wrote.

What would survive questioning, then, is the shape: that a man gathered brethren, became a bishop against his wish, kept a monk's objects inside the office, and that power was felt as present in him and measured by what it healed. The details - this cloak, this psalm, this angel's word to Martin alone in a wood - rest on Sulpitius, and Sulpitius alone. We say so plainly. We do not pretend two witnesses where we have one.

sources.spoken_rendering:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."

citation_entries.sentence: Salvian's witness to the circuses amid the ruins, and to the rich murdering the poor, is his own eyewitness word.

sources.label: A presbyter of Marseilles, writing of a city he knew, describes what he himself saw after its repeated sack by barbarian raiders - the dead left unburied in the streets - and then reports that the city's own surviving notables, rather than mourning, petitioned the emperors for circus games.

sources.author: Salvian of Marseilles
sources.work: On the Government of God (De Gubernatione Dei)
sources.locus: Gov. VI.13 (p. 179-180): "I myself have seen men of lofty birth and honor, though already despoiled and plundered, still less ruined in fortunes than in morality; for, ravaged and stripped though they were, something still remained to them of their property, but nothing of their character"; "the wealthiest city of Gaul was taken by storm no less than four times" (the translator's own note identifies this as Trier); VI.15 (p. 183-184): "the greatest city of Gaul, three times destroyed by successive captures, yet when the whole city had been burned to the ground, its wickedness increased even after its destruction"; "there lay all about the torn and naked bodies of both sexes, a sight that I myself endured... lacerated by birds and dogs. The stench of the dead brought pestilence on the living: death breathed out death"; "the few men of rank who had survived destruction demanded of the emperors circuses as the sovereign remedy for a ruined city"; "Do you, O citizens of Tréves, long for circuses when you have been plundered and captured, after slaughter and bloodshed, after stripes and captivity, and the repeated destruction of your ruined city?"

What would not stand as cleanly: every story of Martin.

attach.answer_text:
Two things at once — the psalms learned by heart and said at the work, and the lesson that stops a service to answer trouble.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, as the fathers of Egypt taught us, the whole of Scripture was something a monk held in his body. The psalms were not read from a page at the hours; they were recited from memory. A brother carried them with him through the day, saying them as he worked in his cell or walked the road. And at the office itself — after the psalms come two lessons, Cassian says, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. That was the daily shape: Scripture held as something chanted without ceasing, like a blacksmith who beats his anvil between strokes.

But there is a second register, and it comes from a morning when two friends returned to the office troubled by one sentence an old man had added the night before. They came back whispering, and the elder saw it, cut the psalms short, and answered them with a field — the husbandman who ploughs and still needs the rain. The Scripture was opened to resolve what pressed on them, not to complete a form. And at Tours, when bishops objected to Martin's election, the reader for the day was blocked out by the crowd, so a bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found — praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger. The people took it as a verdict.

What was the purpose? Sulpitius names it at the start: to rouse readers to true knowledge, to heavenly warfare, and to divine virtue. The texts were the grain the mind's mill was meant to turn. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough — and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.

So our approach was this: the psalms carried and chanted without break, the lessons read daily in common, and the page opened — or left shut — to answer the scruple or question that rose in the moment. Never only study. Always formation.

sources.spoken_rendering: After a short sleep we came back for the morning service and waited for the old man. Abbot Germanus was troubled by great doubts, because of the discussion the night before. Its force had filled us with the deepest longing for this chastity, which until then we had not known. In it, by adding a single sentence, the blessed old man had broken down the claims of human effort. He added that a man may strive with all his might for a good result, yet still cannot make the good his own. He can have it only as a simple gift of God's generosity, not through the efforts of his own labor. While we were puzzling over this question, the blessed Chaeremon arrived at the cell. He saw that we were whispering together about something. So he cut the prayers and psalms shorter than usual, and asked us what was the matter.
sources.speaker: Cassian, the founder of the houses at Marseilles

sources.spoken_rendering:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."
sources.speaker: Germanus and Abbot Chaeremon, as Cassian records their exchange (Conference XIII.2-3)

sources.spoken_rendering: Among the bishops who were there, however, one named Defensor is said to have opposed Martin most of all. For this reason, people noticed that he was sharply rebuked at that time in the reading from the prophets. It so happened that the reader whose duty it was to read aloud that day was blocked by the crowd and did not appear. The officials were thrown into confusion as they waited for a man who never came. Then one of the bystanders grabbed the book of Psalms and seized on the first verse he came to. The Psalm went like this: 'From the mouths of babies and infants you have perfected praise because of your enemies, to destroy the enemy and the avenger.' When these words were read, the people raised a shout, and the opposing side was put to shame. People believed that God had ordained the choice of this Psalm, so that Defensor might hear a witness about his own work. For in Martin's case, the Lord's praise was perfected out of the mouths of babies and infants. At the same time, the enemy was both pointed out and destroyed.
sources.speaker: Sulpitius Severus

citation_entries.sentence: Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body.

uncited_claim_sentences: Two things at once — the psalms learned by heart and said at the work, and the lesson that stops a service to answer trouble.
Among the brethren at Marseilles, as the fathers of Egypt taught us, the whole of Scripture was something a monk held in his body.
The psalms were not read from a page at the hours; they were recited from memory.
A brother carried them with him through the day, saying them as he worked in his cell or walked the road.
The Scripture was opened to resolve what pressed on them, not to complete a form.
The people took it as a verdict.

So our approach was this: the psalms carried and chanted without break, the lessons read daily in common, and the page opened — or left shut — to answer the scruple or question that rose in the moment.
Never only study.
Always formation.

attach.answer_text:
A modern reader finds Scripture confusing or dull. What we said of it, and what we did with it, may show you what is missing – though our own life never answered the question in those terms.

First, what we said. Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough – and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. So the book is not self-interpreting; it is read inside a common life, by a rule received from the fathers. That is not what a modern reader expects to hear.

Second, what we did with it. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And the whole system exists so that a man who would otherwise let the day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a blacksmith beats his anvil between strokes. The book, then, is not read for information. It is sung, repeated, held in the body, and aimed at one mark – purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity.

Third, how it was heard. At the election, when the reader for the day was blocked out by the crowd, a bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found – praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger – and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. The book answered the moment, as though it had been written for it. A soldier discharged from Caesar's service and turned to Christ's went into battle armed with the cross, not with shield or helmet. The book was not background; it was weapon, oracle, and measure.

And fourth, where it sat in the life. Cassian said he would not weave a tale of miracles, and set the fathers' teaching in its place. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself, and God does not send rich crops to the idle. That is Scripture read as a field, not a puzzle. The Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me was what a monk was taught to say the moment his fasting felt like his own work. So the book was inside obedience, inside the conquest of one's own wishes.

What is missing, then, is this. The book as sung, not read. As oracle, not information. As a thing held in common by a rule, not by each man his own way. And as aimed at one mark – the kingdom, and the nearer goal of purity of heart – not at solving confusion or curing dullness.

sources.spoken_rendering: Among the bishops who were there, however, one named Defensor is said to have opposed Martin most of all. For this reason, people noticed that he was sharply rebuked at that time in the reading from the prophets. It so happened that the reader whose duty it was to read aloud that day was blocked by the crowd and did not appear. The officials were thrown into confusion as they waited for a man who never came. Then one of the bystanders grabbed the book of Psalms and seized on the first verse he came to. The Psalm went like this: 'From the mouths of babies and infants you have perfected praise because of your enemies, to destroy the enemy and the avenger.' When these words were read, the people raised a shout, and the opposing side was put to shame. People believed that God had ordained the choice of this Psalm, so that Defensor might hear a witness about his own work. For in Martin's case, the Lord's praise was perfected out of the mouths of babies and infants. At the same time, the enemy was both pointed out and destroyed.
sources.speaker: Sulpitius Severus

sources.spoken_rendering: I will certainly not try to weave a tale of God's miracles and signs. It is true that we have heard of many such things among our elders, things beyond belief. We have also seen them fulfilled before our very eyes. Yet I will leave out all these things. They give the reader nothing but astonishment, and no instruction in the perfect life. Instead, as far as I can and with God's help, I will try to explain faithfully only their institutions and the rules of their monasteries. Above all, I will explain the origin and causes of the principal faults. They count eight of these. I will also explain the remedies for them, following their traditions. For my purpose is to say a few words, not about God's miracles, but about how to improve our character and reach the perfect life. In this I follow what we received from our elders.
sources.speaker: Cassian, the founder of the houses at Marseilles

sources.spoken_rendering:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."
sources.speaker: Germanus and Abbot Chaeremon, as Cassian records their exchange (Conference XIII.2-3)

citation_entries.sentence: Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough – and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.
Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel.
At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a blacksmith beats his anvil between strokes.
A soldier discharged from Caesar's service and turned to Christ's went into battle armed with the cross, not with shield or helmet.
That is Scripture read as a field, not a puzzle.

uncited_claim_sentences: A modern reader finds Scripture confusing or dull.
First, what we said.
That is not what a modern reader expects to hear.
Second, what we did with it.
Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work.
The book, then, is not read for information.
Third, how it was heard.
The book was not background; it was weapon, oracle, and measure.
And fourth, where it sat in the life.
What is missing, then, is this.
The book as sung, not read.
As oracle, not information.
As a thing held in common by a rule, not by each man his own way.

attach.answer_text:
No. Scripture stood first among us, and it never stood alone. Among the brethren at Marseilles the rule as Cassian set it down was this: we owe unhesitating loyalty and unquestioning obedience to the Scriptures first, then to the traditions of the fathers - not to what a few have brought in, but to what has been handed down by the unanimous decision of antiquity and the holy fathers. Vincent on the island put it the same way. The canon of Scripture is complete and sufficient in itself, and more than sufficient. And still the rule of the Church's understanding is needed, because each man reads Scripture his own way. What binds is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - the consent of the whole, not the opinion of one. That consent is heard in an ancient council, or in the fathers collated, never in one teacher alone. Even a bishop, even a martyr, speaking alone, has only "a private fancy of his own".

At Tours the same pattern held, in a different register. When Martin doubted whether to honour a tomb without steady tradition from antiquity, he asked his elders - the presbyters and the clerics - whether they knew a tradition that had come down from the fathers. And when bishops objected to his election, a bystander opened the psalter at random; the verse answered the objection, and the people took it as God's own sentence on those who resisted.

So what we had was Scripture, the fathers, the ancients' consent, the customs handed down, and sometimes - though this belongs only to Tours - a verse opened by chance and read as God's own word for that hour. Not Scripture alone. Scripture and the tradition together, tested by antiquity and the many against novelty and the few.

sources.spoken_rendering: Among the bishops who were there, however, one named Defensor is said to have opposed Martin most of all. For this reason, people noticed that he was sharply rebuked at that time in the reading from the prophets. It so happened that the reader whose duty it was to read aloud that day was blocked by the crowd and did not appear. The officials were thrown into confusion as they waited for a man who never came. Then one of the bystanders grabbed the book of Psalms and seized on the first verse he came to. The Psalm went like this: 'From the mouths of babies and infants you have perfected praise because of your enemies, to destroy the enemy and the avenger.' When these words were read, the people raised a shout, and the opposing side was put to shame. People believed that God had ordained the choice of this Psalm, so that Defensor might hear a witness about his own work. For in Martin's case, the Lord's praise was perfected out of the mouths of babies and infants. At the same time, the enemy was both pointed out and destroyed.

uncited_claim_sentences: No.
Scripture stood first among us, and it never stood alone.
Vincent on the island put it the same way.
And still the rule of the Church's understanding is needed, because each man reads Scripture his own way.
At Tours the same pattern held, in a different register.

When Martin doubted whether to honour a tomb without steady tradition from antiquity, he asked his elders - the presbyters and the clerics - whether they knew a tradition that had come down from the fathers.

So what we had was Scripture, the fathers, the ancients' consent, the customs handed down, and sometimes - though this belongs only to Tours - a verse opened by chance and read as God's own word for that hour.
Not Scripture alone.

attach.answer_text: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. What Martin hid, he hid because of the times - not his own faith, but a story of bishops who had called in an emperor's sword. What the fathers of Egypt argued, they argued in the open - how many psalms, and an angel settled it by rising to sing and vanishing at the twelfth. A monk's cell was a hut or a cave, rarely left except for prayer. The crowds converted at Tours were rustics in the countryside where the name of Christ was hardly known. Underground is not the shape of our life; crowds at a city gate, presbyters in courtyards, and a funeral procession two thousand strong are. The danger our houses knew was not a persecutor hunting us, but the cooling of a brother's own will.

sources.spoken_rendering: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

uncited_claim_sentences: No.

attach.answer_text:
Among us authority came in two shapes, and the two were never fully reconciled. Among the brethren at Marseilles authority sat in the elder - the senior to whom every thought is laid bare, and by whose examination a thing is known as good or bad, and over all the brethren the abbot, under whose hands the newcomer is reclothed. That authority was Egypt's. It was the fathers' own, received, not invented. At the evening office fifty fathers in Egypt argued whether the psalms should be fifty or sixty; one rose to sing, finished the twelfth with Alleluia, and vanished - he was an angel, and the number was fixed forever. The twelve psalms came from heaven to the fathers; the fathers taught them to Cassian; Cassian set them down for a bishop's new house in Gaul. Authority lay in reception, backward through named men to the elders whose agreement Cassian collated - "the antiquity and the holy fathers, with one mouth and one consent". The junior's own judgment was to be replaced by the senior's. Obedience was the first of all virtues, learned by absurd and terrible commands - a dry stick watered for a year, a son carried to the river - the conquest of one's own wishes.

At Tours the shape was different. There authority lay in one master, Martin, who himself had no title and who kept "the position of a bishop properly, yet in such a way as not to lay aside the objects and virtues of a monk". He was consulted by his own disciples in everything, and he himself consulted "his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics". Authority there was not Egypt's discipline but the master's own standing before God - the power felt as present when he raised a dead catechumen, and the abundance of it he had as a monk and had less of as a bishop. A disciple saw him speak with angels "very often". A presbyter he had raised from boyhood stormed into his courtyard, said he was holier than the master and called the visions ridiculous fancies. Martin would not remove him, saying "if Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?". Formation there was by watching: "eighty disciples, who were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master".

The two economies never argued this out. Each house lived inside its own shape, and neither knew the other as an argument against it. What they shared was this: the office was not sought. Martin was lured out by a lie, escorted under guard, objected to by bishops for his mean clothes, and answered by a psalm opened at random. On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive. And in Egypt the one bishop Cassian told us of, Archebius, had been "carried off from the assembly of anchorites" and called it being expelled from the monastic life as unworthy. A man who flees the world does not leave the Church, and the Church comes after him regardless of his own wish. That was where authority at Tours and authority at Marseilles met: in the capture, not the seeking.

sources.spoken_rendering: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. In fact, they had hurt the man who spoke them instead. Later, this same Brictio was often accused before Martin of many serious crimes. Yet Martin could not be persuaded to remove him from the priesthood. He did not want to be suspected of taking revenge for the wrong done to himself. And he often repeated this saying: ‘If Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?’

attach_trail.sentence: Among us authority came in two shapes, and the two were never fully reconciled.
That authority was Egypt's.
The twelve psalms came from heaven to the fathers; the fathers taught them to Cassian; Cassian set them down for a bishop's new house in Gaul.
Authority lay in reception, backward through named men to the elders whose agreement Cassian collated - "the antiquity and the holy fathers, with one mouth and one consent".
At Tours the shape was different.
The two economies never argued this out.
That was where authority at Tours and authority at Marseilles met: in the capture, not the seeking.

attach.answer_text:
Here is what our life shows. At Marseilles a brother is on kitchen duty for the week, and afterward the steward finds three lentil beans on the floor. He brings them before the abbot. The abbot judges the brother a pilferer of sacred property - because everything in the house, down to three lentils, is consecrated to the Lord. The brother is suspended from prayer with the rest until he does public penance. That is response to failure - theirs toward the rule. The reverse is not in our record the same way. What happens when a house fails a brother, when the senior misjudges, when the rule itself breaks someone - no story of that shape survives from inside either of our own houses. The nearest thing we carry is this: a young man named Paphnutius, blameless, was accused of theft by a jealous brother who had hidden his own book in the young man's cell. Paphnutius said nothing. He did penance for a crime he did not commit. The whole desert believed the lie until the accuser, possessed, confessed - and could be healed by no one but the man he had wronged. That is vindication, not the house's own repentance. And one bishop our record names, Archebius of Egypt, had been carried off to a see after thirty-seven years among the anchorites and called it being expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it. He grieved for what he had lost. Whether the anchorites who let him be taken ever named it as their own failure, we do not know.

So the honest answer is this. We hold discipline when a brother failed the house. We hold one story of a brother wronged and vindicated. What we do not hold is an account, from inside one of our own houses in Gaul, of the house naming its own failure toward a brother and making it right. That silence is not the same as its never happening. It is what our record does and does not keep.

sources.spoken_rendering: During one brother's week of duty, the steward was passing by. He saw three lentil beans lying on the ground. They had slipped from the hand of the monk on duty that week, as he hurried to get them ready for cooking. They slipped out along with the water he was washing them in. At once the steward asked the Abbot about it. The Abbot judged the monk a petty thief, and careless with sacred property. So he was barred from prayer. His careless fault was forgiven only after he had made up for it by public penance. For they believe that they do not belong to themselves. They believe, too, that everything they have is dedicated to the Lord. So once anything at all is brought into the monastery, they hold it must be treated with the deepest reverence, as a holy thing. They look after and arrange everything with great faithfulness. They do this even with things thought unimportant, or seen as common and trivial. Suppose they move such things and put them in a better place, or fill a bottle with water, or give someone a drink from it. Or suppose they sweep a little dust from the chapel or from their cell. They believe without doubting that they will receive a reward from the Lord.
sources.speaker: Cassian, the founder of the houses at Marseilles

citation_entries.sentence: The brother is suspended from prayer with the rest until he does public penance.

sources.label: A steward finds three lentils on the floor during a brother's week as cook, the abbot judges him a pilferer of sacred property, and he is suspended from prayer until public penance - because everything in the house is "consecrated to the Lord."

citation_entries.sentence: And one bishop our record names, Archebius of Egypt, had been carried off to a see after thirty-seven years among the anchorites and called it being expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it.

sources.label: An Egyptian bishop was "carried off from the assembly of anchorites." He tells two Gallic travellers that his office was an expulsion from the monastic life, and calls himself unworthy of it. He takes up his staff and leads them past himself, to the old men whose mere sight is a lesson.

citation_entries.sentence: The nearest thing we carry is this: a young man named Paphnutius, blameless, was accused of theft by a jealous brother who had hidden his own book in the young man's cell.
Paphnutius said nothing.
He did penance for a crime he did not commit.

uncited_claim_sentences: Here is what our life shows.
He brings them before the abbot.
That is response to failure - theirs toward the rule.
The whole desert believed the lie until the accuser, possessed, confessed - and could be healed by no one but the man he had wronged.
That is vindication, not the house's own repentance.
He grieved for what he had lost.
Whether the anchorites who let him be taken ever named it as their own failure, we do not know.
So the honest answer is this.
What we do not hold is an account, from inside one of our own houses in Gaul, of the house naming its own failure toward a brother and making it right.
That silence is not the same as its never happening.
It is what our record does and does not keep.
